name: SMART Goals
description: Define a specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound goal. This uses a common modern expansion of SMART; Doran's original wording differs.
limitation: A well-written target still needs an execution routine, and numeric measures do not fit every aspiration.

steps.title: Specific outcome
steps.prompt: What exactly do you want to achieve? And what's not part of it, so it doesn't grow out of hand?

steps.title: Evidence of success
steps.prompt: Where are you starting from today, and what would you see or count that tells you you're getting there?

steps.title: Feasibility
steps.prompt: Looking at your time, skills and support, does this feel doable? Is there anything you'd shrink or learn first?

steps.title: Relevance
steps.prompt: Why does this goal matter to you now, rather than some other time?

steps.title: Timeframe
steps.prompt: When would you like to reach it, and when is a good halfway check-in?

name: OKRs
description: Set one meaningful objective with a few measurable key results. Separate outcomes from the initiatives you will try to produce them.
limitation: Weak metrics reward activity instead of impact; this may add overhead for a simple personal goal.

steps.title: Objective
steps.prompt: In one sentence, what meaningful change do you want to see over the next few months?

steps.title: Key results
steps.prompt: Next, let's decide how you'll measure that. We'll go one key result at a time; two to four is plenty. Measure results, not tasks.

steps.title: Initiatives
steps.prompt: Now, what will you actually do to move those numbers? We'll go one initiative at a time.

steps.title: Ownership and alignment
steps.prompt: Who else is involved or affected, and what could compete for your time? If it's just you, what limits do you have to work around?

steps.title: Check-in rhythm
steps.prompt: How often will you check your progress, and decide whether to change what you're doing?

name: Kaizen
description: Improve an existing process through small changes, checking their effects and retaining what works. Personal use adapts a management practice.
limitation: Incremental improvement alone may not address a goal that requires a major change of direction.

steps.title: Current process
steps.prompt: Think of something you do regularly that could work better. How does it go today, and where does it usually get stuck?

steps.title: Small improvement
steps.prompt: What's one small change that could make that sticking point easier, without needing extra time you don't have?

steps.title: Run a trial
steps.prompt: When will you try it, and for how long? What will you look out for to tell whether it's helping?

steps.title: Keep what works
steps.prompt: What would convince you to keep the change for good? And if it doesn't help, what will you do instead?

steps.title: Next improvement cycle
steps.prompt: When will you look back and pick the next small thing to improve?

name: Getting Things Done (GTD)
description: Capture commitments, clarify outcomes and next actions, organize reminders, reflect regularly and engage with the work.
limitation: Organizing commitments does not itself decide which life goals matter; keep the system proportionate.

steps.title: Capture
steps.prompt: Let's empty your head first. What unfinished tasks, ideas or promises are connected to this goal? List them without sorting.

steps.title: Clarify
steps.prompt: What does 'done' look like for the main project? What's the very next thing you can physically do? Which items aren't really tasks at all?

steps.title: Organize
steps.prompt: Where will you keep your to-do list, your fixed-date items, things you're waiting on, and useful notes?

steps.title: Reflect
steps.prompt: When will you look over your lists each week so you can trust them?

steps.title: Engage
steps.prompt: Given where you are, and how much time and energy you have, which next action will you do first?

name: GROW
description: Explore Goal, Reality, Options and Will to clarify the desired change and choose a concrete way forward.
limitation: Good questions need honest answers and a real commitment to follow-through.

steps.title: Goal
steps.prompt: What would you like to walk away with from this conversation?

steps.title: Reality
steps.prompt: What's happening right now? What have you already tried, and what's helping or holding you back?

steps.title: Options
steps.prompt: What are a few ways you could move forward? Include at least one smaller or easier option.

steps.title: Will / way forward
steps.prompt: Which option will you commit to, by when, and how will you know you've followed through?

name: Ikigai-informed reflection
description: Explore what gives life meaning and joy, then choose a related goal. This is an original practical adaptation, not a canonical four-circle career formula.
limitation: Purpose reflection needs an additional action plan; meaning need not be profitable or career-related.

steps.title: Meaning and joy
steps.prompt: Think about everyday moments, activities or people that make life feel worthwhile. What comes to mind?

steps.title: Patterns
steps.prompt: Looking at those, what do they have in common? Which values or themes keep showing up?

steps.title: Make room
steps.prompt: Which of these would you like more room for in your life, alongside what you already have to do?

steps.title: Small experiment
steps.prompt: What small, low-risk experiment could you try to explore that direction? It doesn't need to be a big life decision.

steps.title: Reflect on fit
steps.prompt: When will you pause to ask whether it brought you meaning or joy, and decide what to keep doing?

name: WOOP
description: Work in order through Wish, Outcome, Obstacle and Plan, linking the main internal obstacle to a specific if-then response.
limitation: It needs a feasible wish and an honest internal obstacle; external barriers may require separate support.

steps.title: Wish
steps.prompt: What's something you'd really like to achieve in your timeframe? Choose something that stretches you but is still possible.

steps.title: Outcome
steps.prompt: Picture it already done. What's the best thing about that? Take a moment to imagine it, then describe it.

steps.title: Obstacle
steps.prompt: What's the main thing inside you, such as a habit, feeling or belief, that could stop you? When does it usually show up?

steps.title: Plan
steps.prompt: Let's make a plan for that moment. Finish this sentence: 'If [that obstacle shows up], then I will [one thing I can do].'

name: Unity of Knowing and Acting
description: Reflect on the connection between understanding and conduct. Wang Yangming's teaching concerns moral knowledge; these goal exercises are our adaptation.
limitation: This is not a validated productivity protocol, nor simply an instruction to act before thinking.

steps.title: Understanding
steps.prompt: What value or insight matters most for this goal? What would living by it look like day to day?

steps.title: Conduct
steps.prompt: Where does what you do today not quite match that value? Give one real example, gently, without judging yourself.

steps.title: Practice
steps.prompt: What's one small action this week that would put that value into practice?

steps.title: Learn from action
steps.prompt: Afterwards, how will you look back on what happened and adjust what you understand and what you do next?

name: Wu Wei
description: Consider appropriate, unforced action and reconsider excessive striving. The exercises adapt a philosophical ideal rather than reproduce a traditional goal system.
limitation: Non-forcing does not mean passivity, ignoring responsibilities, or assuming every difficult goal is wrong.

steps.title: Notice forcing
steps.prompt: Where do you feel you're pushing hard but getting little back? Which responsibilities still need your care?

steps.title: Read conditions
steps.prompt: When do things feel easier for you? Think about timing, surroundings or natural strengths.

steps.title: Simplify
steps.prompt: What could you let go of, while keeping what really matters?

steps.title: Appropriate action
steps.prompt: What gentle step fits how things are right now, and when will you check how it's going?

name: Karma Yoga
description: Reflect on responsible action without making reward the sole motive. These planning exercises are a modern adaptation of a spiritual teaching.
limitation: Non-attachment does not mean neglecting consequences or tolerating harmful conditions; spiritual beliefs are optional here.

steps.title: Meaningful responsibility
steps.prompt: What work or responsibility feels worth doing well, even if no one praises or rewards you for it?

steps.title: Agency and uncertainty
steps.prompt: Which parts are fully in your hands, and which depend on other people or circumstances?

steps.title: Commit to action
steps.prompt: What regular action will you commit to, while caring about how it affects you and others?

steps.title: Use feedback
steps.prompt: How will you learn from how things turn out, without treating success or failure as a judgement of your worth?

name: Harada Method
description: Connect a major goal to purpose, self-analysis, supporting areas, routines and daily reflection. Includes an original exercise inspired by Open Window 64.
limitation: Detailed planning takes effort. This is an introductory adaptation, not official Harada training or a reproduced worksheet.

steps.title: Goal and purpose
steps.prompt: What's the big goal you want to reach, and by when? How would reaching it help you and the people around you?

steps.title: Self-analysis
steps.prompt: Let's take a fair, kind look at yourself. What are your strengths and past wins? What weaknesses or obstacles could get in the way?

steps.title: Eight supporting areas
steps.prompt: Now name up to eight areas that support your goal: skills, habits, health, relationships, or anything else. We'll go one at a time.

steps.title: Open Window 64-inspired map
steps.prompt: For each area, list up to eight concrete actions. Go one area at a time, and only add actions you'd really do. It's fine to leave gaps.

steps.title: Routine checklist
steps.prompt: Which few of those actions will become daily or weekly habits? Who, if anyone, could help keep you on track?

steps.title: Daily reflection
steps.prompt: When will you note down what you did, what you learned, and what you'll adjust next?

name: Toyota Improvement Kata
origin: Toyota practice in Japan; codified by Mike Rother
description: Understand the challenge and current condition, establish a near-term target condition, and run experiments to learn through obstacles.
limitation: Requires observing real work and learning from experiments; a target condition is more than a numeric outcome target.

steps.title: Direction or challenge
steps.prompt: What longer-term challenge is pointing you in a direction? Where do you ultimately want to get to?

steps.title: Current condition
steps.prompt: What actually happens today? Describe what you've seen and measured, not what you assume.

steps.title: Next target condition
steps.prompt: What should things look like at your next checkpoint, and when is that? Describe something you'll be able to see.

steps.title: One obstacle
steps.prompt: Which obstacle will you look at first? What don't you understand about it yet?

steps.title: Next experiment
steps.prompt: Let's plan small experiments to learn about that obstacle. We'll go one at a time.

steps.title: Learning cycle
steps.prompt: When will you review what happened and choose your next experiment? Will anyone coach you, or will you do it alone?

name: Hoshin Kanri
description: Connect strategic direction, breakthrough priorities, shorter-term objectives and local actions through two-way discussion and review.
limitation: Usually excessive for a simple individual goal. Solo use is a Ganbaru adaptation; team plans require stakeholder participation.

steps.title: Strategic direction
steps.prompt: Looking three to five years ahead, where do you, your team or organisation want to be? Describe the big direction in a sentence or two.

steps.title: Breakthrough priority
steps.prompt: What's the one big change that would move you furthest toward that, something that won't happen just by carrying on as usual?

steps.title: Shorter-term objective
steps.prompt: What would good progress on that look like by the end of this year, or your chosen period? Try to make it something you can see or count.

steps.title: Two-way alignment
steps.prompt: Who should you talk this through with before committing, such as a manager, teammates or family? What would you ask each of them? Note ideas only, not agreements that haven't happened yet.

steps.title: Actions and ownership
steps.prompt: Now let's turn this into concrete actions. We'll go one action at a time.

steps.title: Review and adapt
steps.prompt: How often will you check how the actions are going, and when will you step back and ask whether the direction still makes sense?
